deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page: no formulas, computations or derivations. It is a natural-philosophical and epistemological text in two parts.

(1) Conclusion of the 'Erdseele' (earth-soul) argument, continued from p. 37. The previous page set out a criterion: a closed system of interlocking, changing purpose-and-effect relations in a body is best explained by a single ongoing thought process inside that body, provided (1) the purposiveness does not split into partial systems already closed within parts of the body, and (2) there is no reason to place its cause in a larger whole.

This page applies that same criterion to the purposiveness of organisms taken as a whole:
- (a) The purpose-and-effect relations of organic life on Earth do not split into separate systems; everything interlocks. So they cannot be explained by several separate thought processes in parts of the Earth. This is condition (1).
- (b) As far as experience reaches, there is no reason to look for the cause in a larger whole than the Earth. This is condition (2), argued in three points:
  - (b1) These purposes are closed within the Earth: all organisms are made for life on Earth, so the state of the Earth's crust contains all the reasons for their arrangement.
  - (b2) They are individual: by all we know, they do not repeat on other celestial bodies.
  - (b3) They are not fixed over the Earth's life: ever new, more perfect organisms appear. So the cause must be a thought process that is itself progressing to higher stages.
- Conclusion: from the standpoint of exact natural science, understood as explaining nature through causes, assuming an earth-soul is a hypothesis to explain the existence and history of organic nature. Fechner's influence is explicit on the previous page.

(2) An editorial note '((Lücke)) ((Blatt 16))' marks a gap and the start of a new leaf. The epistemological fragment 'I. Wann ist unsere Auffassung der Welt wahr?' (When is our conception of the world true?) then begins.
- Answer: when the connection among our representations corresponds to the connection among things.
- The elements of our picture of the world are entirely different from the elements of the real thing depicted: the former are in us, the latter outside us.
- Only the connections between elements must agree, in the picture and in what it depicts. This sentence is completed on the next page.

Modern gloss: this is a structural-correspondence (isomorphism or homomorphism) account of truth. Truth is preservation of relations, not resemblance of the relata. The next page adds that the account is independent of how finely the picture is grained, and that refining it is not falsifying it. This anticipates Helmholtz's sign theory and Hertz's 'Bilder' theory.
errors: No mathematical errors are possible, since there is no mathematics.
Point (b2), that organic purposiveness is not repeated on other celestial bodies, is an unsupported empirical assumption, stated as such ('nach Allem, was wir wissen').

There is a mild tension in the overall argument. On p. 37, point 3 says that organic arrangements receive no further development within the life of individuals or of lineages, so their cause is not a simultaneously running thought process. Here, (b3) appeals to progressive development over the Earth's history to justify a progressing thought process. The two are reconciled only by the change of time scale, from individual or lineage to the history of the Earth; Riemann does not make this explicit.

results.what: Argument that the purposiveness of organic nature is best explained by a unified, progressing thought process in the Earth (an 'Erdseele'), presented as a scientific hypothesis
results.modern_name: Fechnerian panpsychism / earth-soul hypothesis (teleological natural philosophy)

results.what: Truth of our world-picture defined as agreement of the connections among representations with the connections among things, the elements themselves being entirely heterogeneous
results.modern_name: Structural correspondence theory of truth / representation as relation-preserving map (cf. Helmholtz sign theory, Hertz's Bildtheorie, structural realism)
results.usually_credited_to: Helmholtz (1860s-1878), Hertz (1894); structural realism later (Russell, Poincaré, Worrall)

deep.surprise_reason: This is philosophical text without mathematics. Both the Erdseele/Fechner discussion and the fragment 'Wann ist unsere Auffassung der Welt wahr?' were published by Dedekind and Weber in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke (1876), among the 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts'. Historians of Riemann's natural philosophy (e.g. Scholz, Bottazzini–Tazzioli, Ferreirós) know them well. The structural notion of truth is a nice early instance, but it is already attributed to him.
transcription_corrections: The page number is written '-38.' (with a leading dash), not 'Nat. Ph. 38'.
There is a faint pencil mark '(5)' in the central margin near '((Blatt 16))'; it is not in the transcription.

Otherwise the machine transcription matches the image well, e.g. 'Diese Folgerungen aus unseren Principien', 'zerfallen nicht in einzelne Systeme', 'gleichzeitig zu höheren Stufen fortschreitenden Denkprocesse', 'Annahme einer Erdseele'.
